# EasyAnalysis

> EasyAnalysis is a free, local-first platform for running statistical, machine-learning and
> spatial/geospatial analysis by pointing and clicking — no coding required. You install it on
> your own computer with a single command; it opens in your web browser but computes natively on
> your machine, so your data never leaves it. Live at https://easyanalysis.dev

## What it is

EasyAnalysis lets students, researchers and professionals run rigorous analyses on their own
data without writing code. Open a project, add a dataset, pick what you want to do, click Run,
and read the results — including model metrics and plain-English interpretation. A built-in AI
Co-Analyst can run analyses for you and explain plots and results, grounded strictly in the
tool's own methods and your actual data.

The tool is domain-general and works with any tabular or spatial data. Its founding reference
domain is Finnish National Forest Inventory (NFI/VMI) data for forest trafficability and
tree-growth modelling, but nothing in the core is forestry-specific.

## How to get it

One command, no Docker and no administrator rights. R is downloaded automatically if it is not
already installed.

- Windows (PowerShell): `iwr -useb https://easyanalysis.dev/install.ps1 | iex`
- macOS / Linux: `curl -fsSL https://easyanalysis.dev/install.sh | sh`

The first run installs R packages and takes a few minutes; afterwards it starts in seconds. The
app opens at `http://127.0.0.1:7788`.

## Key features

- **Point-and-click analysis** — no scripting. Nothing computes until you press Run.
- **Runs entirely on your own computer.** There is no analysis server and no upload step: the
  browser is only the interface, and the computation happens in R on your machine. This is a
  privacy property of the architecture, not a policy.
- **Projects** — your work is saved to disk as you go, so closing the app and coming back
  resumes where you stopped. Large spatial files are referenced in place rather than copied.
- **AI Co-Analyst** — ask it to run an analysis, or to explain a plot or a result. It is
  grounded in the app's own data and methods and will not invent numbers or column names.
- **Recommend** — a plain-English read on what your data looks like and which methods suit it,
  before you model.
- **Built-in R console** — optionally run R directly against your data.
- **Cancellable heavy jobs** — large spatial operations run in a separate process so they can be
  stopped.
- **Themes** — several light and dark colour schemes, switchable at any time.

## Data it accepts

CSV, Excel (.xlsx) and delimited text; and spatial formats: GeoTIFF (.tif) rasters, LAS/LAZ
LiDAR point clouds, GeoJSON, GeoPackage (.gpkg) and Shapefiles. Datasets can also be typed or
pasted in from scratch, and edited in a spreadsheet grid.

## Analyses available

- **Statistical models**: linear regression, ANOVA, linear mixed-effects models, logistic
  regression, discriminant analysis (LDA/QDA/WLDA/RLDA/KDA/LLDA/MMC), principal component
  analysis (PCA), generalized additive models (GAM), survival analysis, and statistical tests.
- **Machine learning**: random forest, support vector machines, neural networks, decision trees,
  gradient boosting (XGBoost), classification, and clustering (k-means, hierarchical, PAM/Gower).
- **Spatial, LiDAR and remote sensing**: point-cloud viewing and individual tree detection,
  canopy height models, raster analysis and band maths, terrain analysis (slope, aspect,
  hillshade, curvature, TPI/TRI, roughness), hydrology (flow direction, accumulation, streams,
  TWI), vector operations, zonal statistics, vegetation indices (NDVI, NDWI, NBR, NDRE), and
  satellite data search and download.
- **Other**: time-series analysis, structural equation modelling (SEM), and Bayesian analysis.

Coordinate reference systems are searched against GDAL/PROJ's own database, so any of the ~6,900
non-deprecated EPSG systems can be selected by code or by name.

## How it works (technical)

EasyAnalysis is an R Shiny application that runs locally. The installer fetches R (if needed) and
the required R packages into a private library, then starts the app and opens your browser at a
local address. Statistical methods and spatial operations are each defined in a registry, so the
same runner drives many analyses consistently.

The AI Co-Analyst calls the OpenAI API using tool-calling that invokes the app's own analysis
functions. It is the only component that uses the network, and only when you send it a message.

A browser-only build (R compiled to WebAssembly via Shinylive) was previously offered and is now
**deprecated** — it proved too slow and too limited for real datasets. The local install is the
supported way to run EasyAnalysis.

## Privacy

Your data is read and analysed by R on your own computer and is never sent anywhere. The AI
Co-Analyst sends only what you ask about, plus the current screen's context, to the language
model — and only when you send a message. If you do not use the Co-Analyst, the app makes no
network requests with your data at all.

## How to cite

Gibson, T. C. (2026). EasyAnalysis: point-and-click statistical, machine-learning and spatial
analysis (Version 0.10.16) [Computer software]. https://easyanalysis.dev

Machine-readable citation metadata is in `CITATION.cff` in the repository. Where a screen
implements a published method, that method's own paper is listed on the app's References screen
and should be cited as well — citing the tool does not replace citing the method.
